mechanism: In Core -peertimeout is the master gate for every liveness disconnect, not one timeout among several. ShouldRunInactivityChecks is node.m_connected + m_peer_connect_timeout < now (refs/bitcoin/src/net.cpp:2003-2006), and it guards both InactivityCheck's four rules -- the '!has_received || !has_sent' first-N-seconds rule, last_send + TIMEOUT_INTERVAL, last_recv + TIMEOUT_INTERVAL, and the handshake-not-completed rule (:2008-2058) -- and, less obviously, MaybeSendPing's ping timeout (refs/bitcoin/src/net_processing.cpp:5488-5497, whose own comment says 'To disable the check during testing, increase -peertimeout'). Ours parses -peertimeout into *handshake-timeout-seconds* (src/config-options.lisp:344-346, src/config.lisp:302-310) whose only consumer is check-handshake-timeout (src/networking/peer.lisp:1478-1490). There is no last_recv rule; connection-send-stalled-p (src/networking/connection.lisp:484-490) additionally requires plusp send-queue-bytes, so it is not Core's last_send rule; and the ping half of check-peer-health (:1492-1547) is ungated.
consequence: Smaller than the finding states in one direction and sharper in another. The knob is NOT simply bound to the wrong thing: Core's rule 4 fires when a connection has not completed its handshake by m_connected + m_peer_connect_timeout, which is exactly what check-handshake-timeout computes, so -peertimeout=3 behaves as Core documents and as p2p_timeouts.py expects. What actually diverges is the gating. Raising -peertimeout is Core's documented way to silence liveness disconnects -- Core's own framework writes peertimeout=999999999 into every node's bitcoin.conf (refs/bitcoin/test/functional/test_framework/util.py:570-574) so that mocktime jumps do not disconnect peers -- and under that setting our node still disconnects on an outstanding ping at 1200 s, because our ping timeout is not gated by the knob. In the other direction the residue is benign: at defaults our ping ladder drops a silent peer at about 1320 s where Core's last_recv rule drops it at 1200 s, i.e. strictly more lenient, so no honest peer is lost. The finding's claim that a peer answering pongs while silent for 25 minutes exposes a gap is REFUTED -- a pong refreshes Core's last_recv too, so Core keeps that peer as well. The genuine send-side gap stands: with an empty send queue and nothing accepted by the socket for 21 minutes we judge the connection healthy where Core's last_send rule fires, though in practice pings keep the queue non-empty.

fix_shape: Port ShouldRunInactivityChecks as a predicate over the peer's connect time and *handshake-timeout-seconds*, and make it the gate for every liveness verdict check-peer-health returns -- the ping timeout first, since that is the one an operator or a functional test expects the knob to control. Then complete InactivityCheck as one function evaluated behind that gate: a receive rule on connection-last-recv-time older than 1200 s, a send rule on connection-last-send-time (not on the queue) older than 1200 s, and the existing handshake rule, keeping connection-send-stalled-p as the separate, tighter backpressure signal it is. Both accounting slots already exist and are maintained on every read and write (src/networking/connection.lisp:435-436, :818); today they are read only by getpeerinfo (src/rpc/net.lisp:217-219), so this is wiring rather than new bookkeeping. Leave *handshake-timeout-seconds* named as it is or rename it to the grace period it becomes, but do not change its default: 60 matches DEFAULT_PEER_CONNECT_TIMEOUT. A regression test sets the knob high and asserts no liveness disconnect fires, with the default-knob ladder as the positive control.
